issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the simultaneously severe, poorly processed trauma-memory profile implied by 'Full Sensory Reliving' and 'Olfactory Recall'. Those latter items suggest intrusive sensory re-experiencing, while very easy verbal access points in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile in the same profile without additional context.

The Threat node is not coherent internally: 'Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating' is a non-threat/cognitive impairment item, whereas the other threat items are specific hypervigilant danger-monitoring states ('Waking Alert', 'Startle to Movement'). This makes the Threat selections thematically inconsistent.

Cross-node coherence is weak around 'Triggers: Being Followed'. That trigger implies a persecutory/social-tracking danger theme, but the rest of the profile centers more on restraint, safety checking, startle, and sensory reliving, without corresponding appraisals or memories about pursuit/tracking. It feels insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation.

'Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out' is not well linked to the selected trigger/threat pattern. The profile emphasizes tiredness, restraint sensations, night-time safety checking, and movement-related startle, but not a clear outside/public-space threat theme. Avoiding going out therefore appears mismatched to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Katarina

Katarina was nineteen when the nightclub collapsed. She had been dancing there for eight months, a Friday and Saturday fixture at Prometheus in downtown Milwaukee—a converted warehouse that attracted the city's underground electronic music scene. On a March evening, during the third set, the upper-level mezzanine gave way. The sound was not loud at first; it was a groan, a settling, and then a roar of metal and concrete. She remembered the smell most vividly: dust and rust and something chemical, like burning plastic. The air became thick. Bodies fell around her. She was pinned beneath a section of railing for what felt like hours but was probably twenty minutes, her left arm twisted beneath her, unable to move, unable to call out properly because the dust had filled her mouth and throat. When the firefighters pulled her free, her arm was badly fractured. She spent three days in the hospital. The official investigation concluded that the building's owner had ignored structural reports for years. No charges were filed. The owner settled with some families out of court. Katarina received nothing—her injury was not life-threatening, and her family could not afford a lawyer. What happened to her was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. That injustice sat in her chest like a stone.

In the weeks after discharge, Katarina tried to return to normal. Her arm healed. She went back to her apartment, back to her part-time job at a yoga studio, back to the idea that she would dance again. But something had shifted. She began to notice, with growing dread, that when she felt very tired or exhausted—which happened often, because she was not sleeping well—her mind would flood with the memory of the collapse. The fatigue seemed to open a door. Similarly, when she felt followed or tracked, even in mundane moments like being aware of someone's gaze on her in a crowded room, or when she sensed the brush of someone's hand near her back, she was transported. The feeling of being physically restrained, of pressure on her limbs, could send her spiraling back to that moment beneath the railing. These sensations did not bring her a simple memory; they brought the event back in its entirety, across all her senses at once. The dust returned. The smell of burning plastic filled her nostrils. Her arm ached as if it were being crushed again. She could taste blood. The reliving was so complete and so overwhelming that she had come to believe that if she allowed herself to think about the event, she would not be able to handle it. The thought alone terrified her.

Her fear of what thinking might do to her drove her to avoid the very situations that might trigger those thoughts. She stopped going out. She withdrew from her shifts at the yoga studio, citing illness, until they quietly let her go. She stayed in her apartment with the curtains drawn, where she felt less exposed to the gaze of others, less vulnerable to the sensation of being followed. When she did venture out—to the grocery store, to see her mother—she would cover her face with her hands, pulling her hood up, making herself small. She gave up the pleasant activities that had once defined her: she no longer danced, not even alone in her apartment. She did not go to the coffee shop where she used to study. She did not see her friends. The avoidance felt necessary, a way of keeping the memories at bay, but it also meant that her world was shrinking.

At night, Katarina would wake in a state of high alert, her heart pounding, checking the locks on her apartment door, making sure no one was standing in the shadows. Unexpected movement—a car passing her window, someone shifting in the seat next to her on a bus—caused her to react as if she were in immediate danger, her body flooding with adrenaline before her mind could catch up. This constant vigilance, this sense that threat was imminent, made it impossible for her to concentrate on anything. She would sit down to read or to work on something and find that her attention would scatter, pulled back always to scanning her environment, to listening for sounds that might signal danger. The hyperarousal fed into the avoidance; because staying alert felt so exhausting, because the vigilance made her feel so depleted, she found herself even more drawn to staying home, to limiting her exposure to situations where she might have to maintain that exhausting state of watchfulness. And because she was staying home, because she was not engaging with the world, the triggers seemed to find her anyway. A moment of fatigue would come, and with it the memory. She would feel trapped in her own apartment, and the sensation of restraint would flood back.

Katarina had come to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere. The nightclub was gone; the community she had been part of had scattered. Her friends had moved on, and she did not know how to be around them anymore—did not know how to explain why she could not go out, why she flinched at sudden movements, why she sometimes covered her face and said nothing. Her family worried about her but did not understand. She had tried to return to dance, but her body felt foreign to her now, and the memory of the collapse was too close, too ready to surface. She was nineteen years old and felt utterly displaced, unable to articulate to anyone—perhaps unable even to articulate to herself—what had happened to her and what it had done. She knew what happened, but she could not find the words. When she finally called a trauma therapist, it was not because she had decided she was ready to heal. It was because the isolation had become unbearable, and she was afraid that if she stayed in her apartment much longer, she would disappear entirely.
